verdict: Avoid fresh refining-linked exposure in Paradip; lend only to IOC-anchored service and chemical-supply contractors with tight structure, and decline anything tied to throughput or crude-price upside.
title: Paradip Petroleum Refining & Coal Products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is here
Paradip is a one-anchor town: IndianOil's Paradip Refinery, a 15 MMTPA complex, is the demand engine, and almost every SME we see is a satellite of it — chemical supply, cooling-tower operation, maintenance, logistics, manpower [1]. **The refinery converts crude into product and cash at a margin set by crude spreads, not by anything a local SME controls.** So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower sells to IOC on a purchase order or sells a product whose price floats with crude; if it floats, ask what happens to their receivable and inventory value when crude moves, because the peer set shows margin swings of that size [7]. ## Where value and cash actually sit
Value sits in the refinery's margin and in the working-capital cycle of whoever supplies it. **Our borrowers earn a fixed service or supply margin and carry the receivable — the price risk stays with IOC.** Peer results confirm the margin is real but volatile: HPCL's GRM rose to US$32.2/bbl, up 35% QoQ and 262% YoY, on lower throughput of 6.2 mmt [7]; BPCL's quarter turned on Brent moving from around $70 per barrel [4]; IOC's Q2 beat came on inventory gains [6]. None of that margin accrues to a local vendor. Capex is the refinery's, not the SME's — the visible local spend is tendered opex like cooling-water treatment chemicals and tower operation [3]. **So the credit question is receivable quality and contract tenure, not refining economics.**

## What has changed now
Local news is thin and operational, not financial: a Level-II mock drill simulating a seal leak and fire in the Delayed Coker Unit Fractionator Reflux Pump, run under the refinery's ERDMP [1]. **That tells us the DCU is the unit under scrutiny, so any borrower whose contract touches DCU-adjacent maintenance should be asked about shutdown windows and payment timing.** The macro data is the harder signal: India-wide NIC 19 output is -0.6% YoY and -0.9% Apr-to-date [D], and Odisha's GST collections grew just +0.5% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1%, with electricity demand +5.1% versus +9.5% [D]. **The state is running 5.6 pp behind India on GST and 4.4 pp behind on power — that is a local demand and payment-discipline signal, not a refinery signal.** Note the rating reports are undated and one is from 2017 [8][9][11]; treat them as background only. ## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
Pursue the contracted opex supplier: chemical and cooling-tower operation vendors on live IOC tenders [3], and maintenance contractors with multi-year rate contracts and IOC as direct counterparty. **Avoid traders who buy and resell petroleum product on their own account, and avoid anyone whose repayment depends on crude spreads.** Structure against the purchase order: sanction as a receivables line, not a term loan; covenant that IOC remains the counterparty and that assignment of receivables is executed; take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, monthly GST returns, and quarterly confirmation of outstanding from IOC. **If the borrower cannot produce an IOC purchase order or work order, decline — collect from customer the contract copy and last three months' payment advices.**

## Early-warning signs
- **Monthly:** receivable days against the contract's stated credit period — if days stretch beyond the agreed period, ask for the IOC payment advice and freeze further drawing. - **Monthly:** GST return filing and turnover — if Odisha-level collections stay near +0.5% [D] and the borrower's own filings fall, reduce limit. - **Event-driven:** any shutdown or incident notice at the DCU [1] — if the borrower's scope is affected, ask for the revised schedule before releasing the next tranche.
